title: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook (October 2027) — the Winter Fuels Outlook edition
source: EST: eia.gov/outlooks/steo/release_schedule.php, re-fetched direct 2026-09-08 (HTTP 200, 54,906 bytes) and parsed cell-by-cell by the eia-steo-2026-11-10 never-assessed initial research. Its 2027 rows read, verbatim by cell, `['October 2027', '10/13/2027', 'Winter Fuels Outlook']` and `['November 2027', '11/09/2027', '']` — the Winter Fuels note sits in the trailing Notes column of the OCTOBER row. Release window stated on the same page as 12:00-12:15 pm ET. The date does NOT reproduce from the page's plain rule ("the first Tuesday following the first Thursday of each month"): 2027-10-07 is the first Thursday, so the rule alone yields 10-12, and 10-11 is Columbus Day, a Federal holiday on the Monday before — which by the page's own footnote pushes the release to Wednesday 10-13. So the table and the rule-plus-footnote agree, and the one-week-later-than-usual look is fully explained by the holiday. Filed estimate on two counts, neither of them date doubt: this calendar defines no `confirmed` prefix for the EIA (the standing schema gap eia-steo-2026-09-09 named), and this lane never self-confirms an event it discovered in-sweep
notes: Discovered during eia-steo-2026-11-10's never-assessed initial research (2026-09-08), off the same EIA release-schedule primary that dates the November 2026 edition. Proposed for one reason: it carries this session's correction forward into calendar DATA rather than only into a ledger. That session found the calendar had filed 2026-11-10 as "the Winter Fuels Outlook edition" when four EIA primaries put the Winter Fuels Outlook in OCTOBER every year (2024-10-08, 2025-10-15, the 2026 table's 10/06 Notes cell, and this 2027 row's 10/13) — the error came from reading a trailing-column note as a heading for the row beneath it. Filing the genuine 2027 Winter Fuels edition under its own correct date means the next lane to reach for "which edition carries the winter product" reads the answer from the calendar instead of re-deriving it. The eleven other 2027 STEO dates visible on the same table were DELIBERATELY NOT proposed: both the 2026-10-06 and 2026-11-10 ledgers measure the STEO release as a null for this book (across the eight 2026 editions every tracked name sits at or below its ordinary day; across both reachable November editions, 32 of 32 full-day and 22 of 23 release-hour observations sit inside their own p90), and a measured null does not earn eleven low-impact research jobs. This one earns its place because it carries a corrected fact, not because a STEO date is worth tracking on its own. Filed `low` on the sibling entries' reasoning: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape, and this calendar's names are `symbols: []` away from it.
